title: Foundation of Machine Learning and AI
requirements: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of machine learning and artificial intelligence, covering key algorithms and models.
outcome: By the end of Foundations of Machine Learning and AI, students will understand basic machine learning ideas, e.g. linear regression and classification in terms of loss, likelihood, and decision theory, and explain the architecture of deep neural networks, training via gradient descent and backpropagation. Students will be able to discuss the roles of regularization, convolutional neural networks, autoencoders, and attention/transformers at a conceptual level.
syllabus: This course covers foundational concepts underpinning machine learning and AI. Following a brief review on linear algebra, probability and information theory for ML, various learning models and training will be covered, including single-layer regression/classification, loss/likelihood and MLE, least-squares geometry, bias–variance, discriminant functions/decision theory, and optimization via (stochastic) gradient descent and backpropagation with regularization (weight decay, dropout, learning curves). Selected topics (instructor-added) may include CNNs, autoencoders, and transformers/attention.
recommended_readings: Bishop, C. M., & Bishop, H. (2023). Deep learning: Foundations and concepts. Springer Nature.Bengio, Y., Goodfellow, I., & Courville, A. (2017). Deep learning. MIT press

title: Basic Programming for AI
requirements: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
description: Students will learn essential programming skills using Python, focusing on problem-solving and data analysis techniques applicable to AI.
outcome: By the end of this course, students should be able to: write Python code beyond “notebook hacking” clean messy data, run analyses, and produce figures build reusable modules/classes for research tasks handle errors properly (not crash silently) create reproducible environments that others can run collaborate professionally with Git/GitHub run a baseline machine learning workflow using scikit-learn Specifically, the students can aim to achieve the following objectives:A. Core Python Programming Competence Write correct Python programs using variables, expressions, control flow, loops, and functions to solve data-driven problems. Use Python data structures effectively (lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets) and apply common patterns such as slicing, iteration, list comprehensions, and functional tools (e.g., zip, enumerate, lambda). Work confidently with strings and encodings, including text processing tasks commonly encountered in scientific data and AI pipelines. B. Software Design and Object-Oriented Programming Apply object-oriented programming (OOP) principles—inheritance, encapsulation, abstraction, and polymorphism—to build modular and reusable code. Design basic Python modules and scripts, separating logic into functions/classes and structuring code for clarity and maintainability. C. Practical Engineering Skills for Reliable Coding Debug and interpret Python errors, using error messages, print-based inspection, and systematic debugging strategies to identify and fix issues efficiently. Implement robust programs with error handling, including exceptions, input validation, and defensive coding practices. D. Data Handling and Scientific Computing Read, write, and manage files and datasets, including common formats (CSV/JSON/TXT), using appropriate File I/O techniques. Use NumPy for numerical computing, including array operations, vector/matrix/tensor manipulation, and efficient computation through vectorization. Use pandas for data extraction, cleaning, transformation, and aggregation, preparing datasets for downstream analysis and modelling. E. Visualization and Communication Create clear and informative visualizations using Matplotlib, selecting appropriate chart types and formatting to communicate results effectively. F. Reproducible and Collaborative Workflows Build reproducible Python environments using conda/mamba, manage dependencies, and control randomness using seeds. Collaborate using Git/GitHub, including basic version control operations, branching workflows, pull requests, and code review practices. G. Quality Assurance and Maintainability Improve reliability and code quality using assertions, logging, basic testing (pytest), and (introductory) type hints to support correctness and future extension. H. Applied AI Programming (Tool-Oriented, Not Theory-Heavy) Use common ML/AI Python libraries as practical tools (e.g., scikit-learn and introductory exposure to TensorFlow/PyTorch/Keras) to: a) load and preprocess data, b) train baseline models, c) evaluate performance using standard metrics, and d) run simple end-to-end modelling workflows.

title: Mathematics & Statistics for AI
requirements: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
description: This course provides a solid foundation in the mathematical and statistical concepts necessary for understanding and developing AI models, including linear algebra, probability, and statistical inference.
outcome: Students completing this course gain the mathematical foundations needed to understand, design, and build AI models. They use linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, SVD) to structure data and representations; apply multivariate calculus and computation graphs to derive and implement backpropagation; and wield probability, information theory, and inference to formulate principled objectives (entropy, cross‑entropy, KL). They diagnose conditioning and stability, choose effective SGD/optimizer strategies, and reason about constraints. They reduce dimensionality with PCA, model latent structure via GMM/EM, and leverage the mathematics of CNNs for vision. The result is a disciplined ability to translate real problems into robust, well‑optimized AI systems.

title: Introduction of AI for Science
requirements: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
description: This course explores the transformative applications of AI in research, innovation, and technology across various science disciplines. Through engaging case studies and practical examples, students will discover how AI is reshaping the landscape of modern science and technology. Students will attend lectures featuring different science researchers, who will share how AI has been utilised in their fields. Designed to be accessible, the course emphasizes the practical applications of AI in science without requiring advanced programming skills or in-depth knowledge of AI techniques.
outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to explain how AI is being applied across a range of science disciplines and describe the opportunities and limitations these applications create for research and innovation. They will be able to interpret and discuss real-world case studies presented by researchers, identifying the research questions addressed, the types of data involved, and the role AI plays in generating or validating insights. Students will also be able to outline the history and motivation behind these problems, including why they matter scientifically and how approaches have evolved over time.
syllabus: Core topics cover major AI applications in the sciences, organized around a rotating set of researcher-led talks and case studies. Each talk introduces an applied scientific problem and the AI approach used to address it, without assuming advanced programming. Across the series, students engage with examples from multiple science domains (as determined by the invited speakers) and develop a shared foundation in discussing AI-enabled research in context. The course also includes dedicated weeks for student presentations, where students synthesize one talk/theme, communicate key ideas to peers, and connect it to broader scientific motivation and context. Specific talk topics may change each year.

title: AI for Life Sciences Research and Applications
requirements: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
description: This course is designed for students with foundational science or computational backgrounds seeking to understand how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms life sciences research and applications. No prior experience in life sciences is required. The course aims to provide essential biological principles to AI-driven solutions across five interconnected domains: macromolecular structure determination, cell imaging, bioinformatics, drug discovery, and personalized medicine and nutrition. Students will learn how AI addresses key technical challenges—from protein folding and genomic analysis to clinical trial optimization—while developing competency in interpreting AI outputs in biological contexts. By course completion, students will understand both the capabilities and limitations of AI applications in advancing life science research.
outcome: Students will understand how artificial intelligence (AI) addresses fundamental challenges across the life sciences—from protein folding and cell imaging to genomic analysis, drug discovery, and personalized medicine. They will compare classical and AI-based approaches, interpret AI outputs in biological contexts, and critically evaluate the impact of AI on accelerating scientific discovery while engaging with ethical considerations required for responsible AI development in life science applications.
syllabus: This course explores how AI addresses fundamental challenges across five interconnected domains of life science research. Module 1 covers macromolecular structure—from structural biology fundamentals to AI-driven protein folding and de novo design. Module 2 examines cell imaging, focusing on microscopy principles and how AI facilitates overcoming challenges in cellular microscopy imaging such as noise, resolution, and annotation. Module 3 addresses real-world applications in personalized medicine and nutrition, grounded in ethical frameworks and stakeholder engagement. Module 4 introduces bioinformatics, comparing classical pipelines with AI approaches for genomic and transcriptomic analysis, emphasizing biological data interpretation. Module 5 traces AI's integration throughout drug discovery—from target identification to clinical trial design and optimization. From the modules, students will be able to develop competency in translating AI capabilities to assist in tackling issues in life research endeavors and applications

title: AI for Chemistry
requirements: For students in MSc Artificial Intelligence for Science
description: This course focuses on how artificial intelligence is applied specifically to chemical data and chemical discovery workflows. Building on machine learning concepts covered in the core modules, students will learn chemistry-aware representations (e.g., molecular graphs and 3D conformations), data curation and evaluation strategies (e.g., scaffold splits, dataset bias, uncertainty), and practical modelling pipelines for molecules, reactions, and spectroscopy. Through case studies and hands-on exercises using Python and chemistry toolkits such as RDKit (and modern deep learning frameworks), students will develop the ability to design reliable AI workflows for real chemical problems including molecular property prediction, reaction outcome modelling, catalyst screening, and data-driven discovery. The course features an invited seminar session delivered by a guest speaker. Students will undertake an individual or group project and give a presentation in the final week.
outcome: Describe the unique characteristics and challenges of chemical data that influence how AI methods are applied in chemistry. Recognise and use common chemistry representations (e.g., SMILES, molecular graphs, basic 3D conformations) and apply standard preprocessing and data curation practices. Apply chemistry-aware evaluation strategies (e.g., scaffold splitting) and identify common issues such as data leakage, dataset bias, and uncertainty in model predictions. Interpret and compare representative AI approaches for key chemistry tasks (e.g., molecular property prediction, reaction prediction/retrosynthesis, and molecule generation) using case studies and guided exercises. Complete a small-scale individual or group project that applies course concepts to a chemistry dataset, and communicate the main results and limitations in a final presentation.
syllabus: Core topics include: (1) unique characteristics of chemical data and why chemistry AI differs from generic ML; (2) chemistry-aware representations and preprocessing (SMILES, molecular graphs, basic 3D conformations, data curation/standardisation); (3) reliable evaluation in chemistry (scaffold-based splitting, data leakage, dataset bias, and uncertainty awareness); (4) representative AI approaches and case studies for molecular property prediction, reaction prediction/retrosynthesis, and constraint-aware molecular generation; and (5) guided hands-on exercises and a small-scale project with final presentation, with optional enrichment via an invited research seminar.
